subject: Computing Hessian when the cost function consists of elementary functions

messages.author: 36881ef030206e12
messages.subject: Computing Hessian when the cost function consists of elementary functions
parts:
Hi all

I am trying to use the stan C++ autodiff library for my visual pose tracking algorithm. Essentially I have a (reasonably complex) non linear cost function that warps a reference image and computes a difference measure between the warped and reference image. The parameters to my warp are defined by a 6 element vector (3 for translation, and 3 for rotation)

I have been able to get the Jacobian of my cost function using stan, but I'm stuck at trying to obtain the hessian. The crux of the problem comes down to elementary functions like sin and cos trying to operate on the stan::math::fvar<stan::math::var> template parameters. If I modify my code to explicitly use the .val() method to obtain the stan::math::var element, although the code compiles, I think the gradients aren't propagated, and so I get incorrect (0) jacobians and hessians.

Could someone please point me how to go about solving this issue? I tried to look at the sample code in earlier posts and unit test code, but they all use Eigen matrix elements, and not the simpler methods such as sin, cos, log. Is it the case that the master branch hasn't implemented the nested templatized math functions?

Thanks a lot!

Regards
Shaurya

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Computing Hessian when the cost function consists of elementary functions
parts:
See:

stan/math/mix/mat/functor/hessian.hpp

The individual fvar<T> functions have not been deeply tested
in most case, so anything involving fvar should be taken as
alpha or beta code. Having said that, you can use

stan/math/prim/mat/functor/finite_diff_hessian.hpp

to test.

- Bob

  template<typename Derived> Derived operator()(

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Computing Hessian when the cost function consists of elementary functions
parts:
Apologies for not providing the full example code. Adding the sin namespace didn't help,
error: invalid initialization of reference of type ‘const stan::math::var&’ from expression of type ‘stan::math::fvar<stan::math::var>’

---

#include <cmath>
#include <stan/math.hpp>
#include <iostream>
#include <Eigen/Dense>
#include <stan/math/mix/mat/functor/hessian.hpp>
#include <stan/math/prim/mat/functor/finite_diff_hessian.hpp>

struct test_functor {

template<typename Derived> Derived operator()(
      const Eigen::Matrix<Derived, Eigen::Dynamic, 1>& theta) const {

using stan::math::sin;
    return sin(theta(0)*theta(1));
  }

};

int main() {
  Eigen::Matrix<double, Eigen::Dynamic, 1> theta = Eigen::Matrix<double,
      Eigen::Dynamic, 1>::Constant(6, 0), G = Eigen::Matrix<double,
      Eigen::Dynamic, 1>::Zero(6);
  Eigen::Matrix<double, Eigen::Dynamic, Eigen::Dynamic> H = Eigen::Matrix<
      double, Eigen::Dynamic, Eigen::Dynamic>::Zero(6, 6);
  test_functor f;
  double cost;
  stan::math::hessian(f, theta, cost, G, H); // <-- This fails
  std::cout << "Gradient computed is " << G << " and Hessian is " << H;
  return 0;
}

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Computing Hessian when the cost function consists of elementary functions
parts:
Instead of your current includes, use this:

#include <stan/math/mix/mat.hpp>
#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>

I was able to get it to run by doing that. In order to get your code to work with the finite_diff_hessian() functor, you'll also need to add "using std::sin;" to the operator() you've definited.

The stan/math.hpp include only includes reverse mode (that should be clear in the autodiff paper, but it's a long read and we don't describe how to use forward mode there).
We've now moved to having these includes:
- stan/math/prim/{scal, arr, mat}.hpp for primitives without using autodiff. scal is for scalar functions (no std::vector or Eigen), arr is for vector (std::vector, but no Eigen), and mat is for Eigen and std::vector.
- stan/math/rev/{scal, arr, mat}.hpp for reverse mode autodiff. stan/math.hpp includes stan/math/rev/mat.hpp
- stan/math/fwd/{scal, arr, mat}.hpp for forward mode autodiff.
- stan/math/mix/{scal, arr, mat}.hpp for mixed mode autodiff. This is what you need. Since you're using Eigen, you'll need to bring in the mat.hpp file.

We really need to add instructions on how to use forward mode and mixed forward / backward mode autodiff.



Daniel

On May 10, 2016, at 12:09 PM, Kumar Shaurya Shankar <kumar....@gmail.com> wrote:

a. Oh! So THAT's what all the subfolder hierarchy is for. It all makes sense now.
b. So that means I checkout the develop branch? stan/math/mix/mat.hpp is not in release (2.9.0)

On Tuesday, 10 May 2016 11:48:12 UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
Instead of your current includes, use this:

#include <stan/math/mix/mat.hpp>
#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>

I was able to get it to run by doing that. In order to get your code to work with the finite_diff_hessian() functor, you'll also need to add "using std::sin;" to the operator() you've definited.

The stan/math.hpp include only includes reverse mode (that should be clear in the autodiff paper, but it's a long read and we don't describe how to use forward mode there).
We've now moved to having these includes:
- stan/math/prim/{scal, arr, mat}.hpp for primitives without using autodiff. scal is for scalar functions (no std::vector or Eigen), arr is for vector (std::vector, but no Eigen), and mat is for Eigen and std::vector.
- stan/math/rev/{scal, arr, mat}.hpp for reverse mode autodiff. stan/math.hpp includes stan/math/rev/mat.hpp
- stan/math/fwd/{scal, arr, mat}.hpp for forward mode autodiff.
- stan/math/mix/{scal, arr, mat}.hpp for mixed mode autodiff. This is what you need. Since you're using Eigen, you'll need to bring in the mat.hpp file.

We really need to add instructions on how to use forward mode and mixed forward / backward mode autodiff.



Daniel




On Tue, May 10, 2016 at 11:32 AM, Kumar Shaurya Shankar <kumar....@gmail.com> wrote:
Apologies for not providing the full example code. Adding the sin namespace didn't help,
error: invalid initialization of reference of type ‘const stan::math::var&’ from expression of type ‘stan::math::fvar<stan::math::var>’

---

#include <cmath>
#include <stan/math.hpp>
#include <iostream>
#include <Eigen/Dense>
#include <stan/math/mix/mat/functor/hessian.hpp>
#include <stan/math/prim/mat/functor/finite_diff_hessian.hpp>

struct test_functor {
  template<typename Derived> Derived operator()(
      const Eigen::Matrix<Derived, Eigen::Dynamic, 1>& theta) const {
    using stan::math::sin;
    return sin(theta(0)*theta(1));
  }
};

int main() {
  Eigen::Matrix<double, Eigen::Dynamic, 1> theta = Eigen::Matrix<double,
      Eigen::Dynamic, 1>::Constant(6, 0), G = Eigen::Matrix<double,
      Eigen::Dynamic, 1>::Zero(6);
  Eigen::Matrix<double, Eigen::Dynamic, Eigen::Dynamic> H = Eigen::Matrix<
      double, Eigen::Dynamic, Eigen::Dynamic>::Zero(6, 6);
  test_functor f;
  double cost;
  stan::math::hessian(f, theta, cost, G, H); // <-- This fails
  std::cout << "Gradient computed is \n" << G << "\n and Hessian is \n" << H;
  return 0;
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Computing Hessian when the cost function consists of elementary functions
parts:
How many dimensions do you have? At the very least,
it's going to require N^2 * 20 bytes plus about 40
bytes per operator/function call in computing the function
and its gradient.

The reason to use autodiff is that finite differences
have low precision and you need to nest one inside the other
to calculate Hessians. We only use the finite diffs to
validate our higher-order autodiff code---we don't recommend
using them for real work.

The hessian() code does call recover_memory() after each row
is computed. We should probably modify it to define H(i,j) = H(j,i)
just to make sure everything's symmetric.

- Bob

>>> - stan/math/prim/{scal, arr, mat}.hpp for primitives without using autodiff. scal is for scalar functions (no std::vector or Eigen), arr is for vector (std::vector, but no Eigen), and mat is for Eigen and std::vector.
>>> - stan/math/rev/{scal, arr, mat}.hpp for reverse mode autodiff. stan/math.hpp includes stan/math/rev/mat.hpp
>>> - stan/math/fwd/{scal, arr, mat}.hpp for forward mode autodiff.
>>> - stan/math/mix/{scal, arr, mat}.hpp for mixed mode autodiff. This is what you need. Since you're using Eigen, you'll need to bring in the mat.hpp file.
